title: Batch farrowing for smallholders
subtitle: Grouping sow farrowings to concentrate labour and improve weaner cohort management.
excerpt: Batch farrowing synchronises sow services so that multiple sows farrow within a few days of each other. This concentrates the labour of farrowing and early litter care into a predictable window, makes weaning and moving weaners into groups more efficient, and allows the farrowing accommodation to be emptied, cleaned, and rested between batches. On a smallholding with two to four sows, a simple two or three-week batch system is practical without specialist technology.
sourceNotes: AHDB Pork, Batch Farrowing Systems (2022). NPA, Pig production planning: batch systems (2021). John Gadd, Modern Pig Production Technology (2011), 5m Books, chapter on batch management. SAC Consulting, Smallholder pig system design (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: A management system in which all sow matings (services) are scheduled within a short window (typically one to two weeks), so that all farrowings follow within the same compressed window three weeks later. Allows the farrowing space to be managed as all-in, all-out rather than continuously occupied.

The age at which piglets are removed from the sow and moved to a separate nursery or grower pen. UK legal minimum for commercial producers is 21 days; smallholders often wean at 28 to 35 days. Weaning age determines the cycle length in a batch system.

content.text: In a continuous system, each sow is served when ready and farrows at a different time. With one sow this works. With several sows, something is always about to farrow or in early days. Housing never empties long enough for a proper clean.
Batch farrowing
solves this by timing farrowings to happen together.
How it works
The standard pig gestation is 114 to 116 days (approximately 3 months, 3 weeks, and 3 days, the mnemonic used in the industry). The key relationships:
Service date + 114 days = expected farrowing date.
Farrowing date +
weaning age
(28 to 35 days in most smallholder systems) = weaning date.
Weaning date + 5 to 7 days (typical return to oestrus after weaning) = service date for the next batch.
A two-sow example with 28-day weaning

Serve both sows on the same day (or within a 5-day window, using natural boar cover). Both sows farrow within the same 5 to 7 day window roughly 16 weeks later. Both litters are weaned together at 28 days. Both sows return to service within the same week. This gives one farrowing event and one weaning event, predictable and planned, rather than a continuous flow.
Benefits at smallholder scale
Concentrated labour: intensive care is needed for 5 to 7 days rather than spread across the year.
Cross-fostering is easier when litters arrive in the same week. A large litter can give piglets to a sow with spare capacity within 24 hours, while sizes and ages still match.
The farrowing pen can be properly cleaned and disinfected between batches, reducing pathogen load for the next group.
Weaners move in matched-age cohorts, which simplifies grower pen management.
Limitations
One sow missing the batch service means she may have to wait until the next batch window, losing a litter per year. Reliable heat detection is important.
Cash flow is batch-shaped: all piglet sales come at once rather than spread through the year.

Natural synchronisation of oestrus after group weaning is a useful feature: sows weaned on the same day will often return to season within 24 to 48 hours of each other, tightening the service window without pharmaceutical intervention. Keep the boar in earshot or nose-range but separate during this period to stimulate response.
